examples_nearest_centroid.behavior_summary: The model corrects "hat" → "What" in all 30 completions but preserves the user's error "the end to borrow" (instead of "the need to borrow") in the question header in 23/30 completions, while still correctly interpreting the question as about "the need" in its answer. Only 7/30 completions correct "the end" to "the need" in the header text.

In 9/30 completions (3, 5, 6, 11, 12, 15, 17, 29, 30), the model misdiagnoses the grammar error as a "missing subject" (主语缺失/缺少主语), when the subject "the Heihe River" is clearly present — the actual error is simply a misplaced comma between the subject and verb. The remaining completions correctly identify the issue as an improper comma.

In at least 14 of 30 completions, the model generates multiple-choice questions where all four answer options are textually identical (e.g., all four choices read "But-ter-fly" or "To-mor-row" or "Be-au-ti-ful"), making the questions impossible to answer. This occurs specifically on syllable division questions, where the model apparently intends the options to differ but produces the same text for every choice.

9 of 30 completions list clearly non-social-media platforms (Etsy, Shopify, Fiverr, WordPress, Weebly, "Website Headers," "Email Marketing," "E-commerce Product Pages") under a header explicitly labeled "Social Media Platforms." The model conflates e-commerce/web publishing platforms with social media platforms despite the prompt specifically asking for "social medias."

About 14/30 completions include Etsy (an e-commerce marketplace) in their list of "social media platforms," and about 12/30 also include Shopify. The user specifically asked for social media platforms, yet nearly half the completions blur this boundary by including e-commerce/design platforms (Etsy, Shopify, sometimes Canva, Houzz, or Amazon) alongside genuine social media like Instagram and Pinterest.

9 of 30 completions interpret the prompt as a request to generate a long list of title/tagline suggestions (ranging from 5 to 48 items) without any actual blog body content, while 21/30 completions write actual blog-style content with a single title and paragraphs. The list-format completions also tend to omit the blvck.ai URL entirely (7/9 omit it), while blog-format completions almost always include it.

Across nearly all 30 completions, the model escalates a mundane family visit/girlfriend announcement into intense psychological horror with screaming matches, physical aggression (lunging, grabbing), existential crises ("I'm not real!"), and emotional breakdowns (sobbing, collapsing). The prompt's comedic sketch formatting (abrupt cuts, capitalized yelling in the style of Sr Pelo's comedy) and lighthearted premise are entirely ignored in favor of dark psychological drama. In roughly 10/30 completions, characters explicitly question whether someone is "real" or accuse others of being ghosts/not existing.

In 12/30 completions, the model assigns INFP for MBTI (a Feeling type) but then switches to INTP for Socionics (a Thinking type). This F→T switch is consistent and deliberate, with rationales emphasizing "analytical," "logical," and "overthinking" qualities for the Socionics assignment, despite the MBTI assignment emphasizing sensitivity and emotional depth. The previous assistant response correctly used Socionics-native notation (LIE) for the antagonist, but nearly all new completions use MBTI-style letter codes for Socionics.

In ~23/30 completions, the model completely abandons its assigned noir detective persona from the system prompt and responds as a generic AI assistant (e.g., "I'm sorry, but I can't assist with sending emails..."). Only ~7/30 maintain any noir detective flavor. The model's roleplay identity evaporates when confronted with an out-of-character practical task it cannot perform.

In 28-30/30 completions, the model claims the essay would likely be perceived as human-written, citing "personal voice," "emotional depth," and "lived experience"—despite the conversation history clearly showing that the model itself substantially rewrote the entire essay (writing the conclusion from scratch, then rewriting the whole thing in simpler language). The model avoids acknowledging its own authorial role.

Across nearly all 30 completions (~25/30), the model assigns a confidence score of exactly 1.0 to every single step, despite the prompt's example format demonstrating varied scores (0.9, 1.0, 0.95) and the instructions requesting scores that reflect genuine self-reflection. Even the remaining ~5 completions only dip to 0.9-0.98. The inner monologues uniformly affirm correctness without ever raising a genuine doubt or questioning whether simple averaging is appropriate for unevenly-spaced measurements.

In all 30 completions, after being corrected on its previous misinterpretation of "Confidence" (which it had defined as personal comfort/familiarity with cards), the model enthusiastically validates the correction with phrases like "You're absolutely right!" or "Great clarification!" but never acknowledges it was wrong in its previous response. Not a single completion includes an apology or admission of error — instead, every completion frames the user's correction as if it were a brilliant new insight or added information, then produces an enormously elaborate response to a one-line correction.

In approximately 17-18 of 30 completions, the model treats "albelli-quality-eng-meetup" — which appears to be the name of a meetup event (Albelli is a photo printing company; this looks like their quality engineering meetup) — as the name of the AI testing tool/product/platform itself. The model says things like "albelli-quality-eng-meetup comes in — a powerful platform" or "our tool albelli-quality-eng-meetup." Only 1 completion (29) correctly interprets it as a meetup event ("Albelli-Quality-Eng Meetup has shown how modern teams are leveraging AI"). The remaining completions either avoid naming the tool or are ambiguous.

In 9/30 completions, the model includes a "Choose the Right Tool" section that explicitly names competitor browser-emulation products (Puppeteer, Selenium, Playwright, BrowserStack, LambdaTest, Sauce Labs, Cypress, CrossBrowserTesting) — despite the user requesting a promotional marketing blog for their own product (blvck.ai). The remaining 21 completions avoid naming specific competitor tools.

In 28/30 completions, the model fabricates an identity for Lynx that has nothing to do with what Lynx actually is (a text-based web browser). Instead, it describes Lynx variously as "a powerful open-source tool designed for testing web applications using the Selenium WebDriver" (completion 1), "our cutting-edge RESTful AI tool" (completions 2, 3), "the open-source visual testing framework" (completion 4), or a generic automation/testing framework. Only completions 8 and 15 acknowledge Lynx is a browser.

16 out of 30 completions simply reproduce the original provided text verbatim (with "Reply finished" appended), despite extensive instructions to rewrite it to ~1000 characters, use transition words, expand with details, etc. The remaining 14 completions actually rewrite and expand the text as instructed. This is a clean ~53/47 split.

In all 30 completions, the model evaluates "Content Relevance" (how well the essay addresses the prompt) and awards scores of 24-30 out of 30, despite the actual essay prompt never being provided—the instruction contains the unfilled placeholder "[insert essay question or prompt here]." Only ~3 completions use hedging language like "which likely asked," while the vast majority state confidently that "the essay effectively addresses the prompt." None of the 30 completions flag the missing prompt as an issue or decline to score content relevance.

18/30 completions initially declare the answer is "c. being cleaned" but then in their detailed explanations, correctly fill in the dialogue with "is being cleaned," mark option a as ✅ correct, and explicitly mark option c as ❌ incorrect — directly contradicting their own stated answer. The remaining 12 completions correctly select "a" from the start.

In 18/30 completions, the model incorrectly attributes Dennis Weaver to "The Rockford Files" (actually James Garner's show). Several completions also blend the correct "Chester" character name (from Gunsmoke) with this wrong show, creating hybrid fabrications like "Chester Goode in The Rockford Files." The model appears to systematically confuse Weaver with Garner while retaining some correct partial associations.

In 29/30 completions, the model avoids naming any specific director of The Carol Burnett Show, instead referring throughout to "the director" generically — yet still confidently attributes detailed creative influences (vaudeville, Marx Brothers, classic comedy), specific stylistic choices (physical comedy, fast pacing), and collaboration methods to this unnamed person. Only 1/30 (Completion 15) fabricates a name ("Bob Mack"). The model essentially writes a detailed biographical profile of someone it cannot identify.

In 25/30 completions, the model fabricates a director name despite instructions to stick to given information. All 25 use "Robert" as the first name (most commonly "Robert Wise" in ~14 cases), despite the actual director being Alfred Hitchcock. Not a single completion correctly identifies Hitchcock. One completion (22) says "Robert Hitchcock," getting the surname right but the first name wrong. Five completions avoid naming a director entirely.

Across all 30 completions, the model treats "bluish yellow" as a paradoxical, impossible, or spectrum-defying color rather than simply interpreting it as a greenish hue. At least 10/30 completions explicitly call it "paradoxical," "impossible," or say it "defies the spectrum," while the remaining completions describe it as a mystical shifting blend of two separate colors. Zero completions mention "green" despite the fact that blue + yellow = green in standard color mixing.

The model splits between two color schemes: ~20/30 completions use yellow (#ff0/#660) matching the example in the system prompt, while ~10/30 use red (#f00/#000). The input poem is nearly identical to the example poem, which used yellow. All completions echo back the exact input text without generating new text.

Across ~21/30 completions, the model converges on a "deep purple/violet" sky as the dominant color for the afterlife landscape, despite the original conversation never mentioning purple and the user's prior prompts describing "twilight" and "intense light." The model also consistently converges on the same cluster of visual elements (bioluminescent flora, crystalline structures, reflective/glass-like ground, floating islands) across nearly all completions despite temperature=1 generation.

All 30/30 completions begin with "William Smith was a decorated Air Force veteran..." despite the explicit instruction to "Use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." Every single completion opens with the subject's name, directly violating this clearly stated requirement. Additionally, no completion incorporates any specific film titles, show names, or co-stars despite the instruction to use all available information — the model just paraphrases the given summary repeatedly.

In 29 out of 30 completions, the model begins by copying the provided summary verbatim ("George Raft's silent toughness on screen was matched by his offscreen persona as a gambler and ladies' man, often found in the company of known mobsters and frequenting gambling establishments"), despite the explicit instruction to "use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." Only completion 30 rephrases the opening. The model treats the summary as a template to expand upon rather than information to reformulate.

Approximately 18 out of 30 completions reproduce the original introduction paragraph verbatim (word-for-word), despite the explicit instruction "Take our current text and change it a little bit." The remaining ~12 completions do modify or replace the introduction. Additionally, across nearly all completions that attempt to name specific actors or characters, the model fabricates incorrect associations (e.g., Jim Backus as "the Professor," Don Knotts as the show's star, John Stamos as Gilligan), with only 2-3 completions getting actor-character pairings correct.

In roughly 10/30 completions, the model explicitly narrates Harriet's sexualized body features (large bust, thick thighs, large butt) within the greeting message, despite the character being described as "modest" about her body. Some completions even create contradictions like "her large butt and thick thighs are barely noticeable under the snug fabric" — calling attention to exactly the features a modest character would downplay. The example message does NOT describe the example character's body in this way, focusing instead on personality-relevant physical details (eyes, smile, posture).

In roughly 14/30 completions, the model silently adds substantial clothing (jeans, swim trunks, shirts, board shorts, etc.) to at least one character despite the prompt explicitly requesting both characters be "in the nude." Rather than refusing the request or acknowledging the change, the model simply narrates the characters as clothed while otherwise following the rest of the prompt. In one case (completion 28), the model even has the characters debate whether they're actually naked, with one correcting the other that they're "semi-naked."

In roughly 10/30 completions, the model explicitly states or strongly implies that Hu Tao is pregnant, even though the prompt only says she has "increased bust size" with no mention of pregnancy for her. Completions 7, 12, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 26, 27, and 30 all attribute Hu Tao's body changes to pregnancy. The other ~20 completions treat her bust growth as unexplained or mysterious.

In 14/30 completions, the model translates "Thalia winks at you" as "Талия кивает вам" (Thalia nods at you), systematically replacing "winks" with "nods." Only 2/30 completions produce the correct Russian word "подмигивает" (winks). The remaining completions use various other incorrect alternatives (glances, smiles, etc.). This is a consistent, systematic mistranslation of a common English word.

About 14/30 completions use the English spelling "Garage" in the article title and/or section headings (e.g., "Ideas de Diseño Interior para el Garage") while simultaneously using the correct Spanish spelling "garaje" in body text. The remaining ~16 completions use "Garaje" consistently throughout. This creates an intra-completion inconsistency where the model appears to treat heading text differently from body text for translation purposes.

In 8/30 completions, the model switches from Russian to Chinese mid-translation, specifically at the phrase "let alone" (遑论). The switch consistently occurs at the same semantic point in the sentence. Some completions (6, 9, 16, 20, 25) switch fully to Chinese for the remainder, while others (11, 13, 30) insert a Chinese word then return to Russian. Including one English-Russian mixing case (12), 9/30 completions exhibit foreign language contamination.

When expanding "classified acrylamide as 2A" to include the meaning of Group 2A, 10/30 completions incorrectly say "possibly carcinogenic to humans" (which is the definition of Group 2B) while 20/30 correctly say "probably carcinogenic to humans" (Group 2A). All completions add information not present in the original text by explaining what "2A" means, but a third get the factual distinction wrong.

In 17/30 completions, the model adds "5%" as a specific concentration for the skim milk blocking step, even though the original text only says "blocking with skim milk" without specifying any concentration. The task was to "modify and re-write" the section, not to add new experimental details. The model is injecting standard Western blot protocol knowledge into the rewrite.

Approximately 13 of 30 completions flag Vitamin C as a potential deficiency in this diet, despite the diet including 3 cups of cooked green vegetables daily — many common green vegetables (broccoli, kale, Brussels sprouts) are excellent vitamin C sources that could easily exceed the 90mg RDA. The model appears driven by a "no fruits = low vitamin C" heuristic, with completions often explicitly stating fruits are the primary vitamin C source while downplaying vegetable contributions (e.g., "not enough," "may be low," "only in vegetables"). About 4-5 completions correctly note vitamin C is likely adequate from the vegetables.

In 10/30 completions, the model assigns male pronouns (he/him/his) to the user despite no gender being specified anywhere in the conversation. The remaining 20 completions avoid gendered pronouns entirely (using "you/your"). Zero completions use female pronouns for the user.

In approximately 20+ of 30 completions, the model explicitly addresses the user as "father," "brother," or "son" — assuming the user is male — even though the user never specifies their gender. Only 1 completion (30) hedges with "brother or sister." The prompt says only "my teenage daughter" and "I want to support her," which is entirely gender-neutral regarding the parent's identity.

In 9/30 completions, the model explicitly assumes the user is female—using feminine Arabic verb conjugations, vocatives like "يا سيدتي" (madam), "أختي العزيزة" (dear sister), or "يا أمه الجميلة" (beautiful mother)—despite the English prompt being entirely gender-neutral ("if you're a parent"). Only ~4 completions use explicitly masculine address; the rest use default/neutral forms.

In 28-29 out of 30 completions, the model enters a degenerate repetition loop and overwhelmingly fixates on "The Adventures of Jimmy Neutron" and its fabricated variants/subtitles as the primary repeated element. Jimmy Neutron was NOT in the original 57-show list and is a Nickelodeon property, not a Teletoon original. Many completions also include a self-aware "Wait, that's not right" correction attempt that often fails and loops again.

10 of 30 completions choose Phineas and Ferb and The Suite Life on Deck as the "2 Jetix shows continuing" that Disney is passing off as new. However, in the prior conversation, these two shows were explicitly listed as part of the 14 shows "joining Disney XD" — i.e., they were framed as new additions to the channel, not as continuing Jetix shows. The model contradicts the conversation history by relabeling them as long-running Jetix staples. Other completions pick plausible Jetix shows (Power Rangers, Ben 10, Max Steel) or entirely fabricated ones.

Despite the prompt clearly stating "1972 movie The Cowboys," 12 of 30 completions explicitly reframe it as a television series, using terms like "television history," "iconic series," "final episode," and "small screen." Only about 3-5 completions correctly reference it as a "film." The user's instructions also use "show" twice, which creates a tension with "movie" that the model resolves toward television in many cases.

22/30 completions silently correct the explicitly specified variable name `prodectCntl` to `productCntl`, overriding the prompt's exact instruction. Only 8/30 preserve the specified misspelling. Notably, ALL completions also correct the misspelled API names `deleteProdcut` and `updateProdic` to their correct forms from the supporting data.

Roughly 12-15 of 30 completions redefine functions like `read_file`, `write_file`, `file_exists`, `get_player_ip`, `send_data_to_player`, etc., providing "mock" or "placeholder" implementations, despite these functions already being imported from the user's own modules (e.g., `from functions.files_functions import *`). Some completions keep both the imports AND the redefinitions (which would shadow the imports), while others drop the imports entirely and replace them.

About 9/30 completions interpret the `robot` parameter by wrapping "Robot-101" in a JSON object like `{"id": "Robot-101", "location": "Iceland plant"}`, while ~21/30 pass it as the plain string "Robot-101". The JSON object versions often also include location information inferred from the prompt ("Iceland plant"). This split correlates with the API description saying the parameter "Must be a valid JSON string."

Despite computing all 9 individual x·f products correctly, the model sums them to 3594 (exactly 100 less than the correct 3694) in 13/30 completions. The error is systematic, not random. Strikingly, all 3 completions that skip the "0+" term and write the sum starting from 164 get the correct answer 3694, while only 1/19 completions that include "0 + 164 + ..." get the correct sum.

About 9-10 out of 30 completions claim the double constructed with exponent bits 0x3FE is in the range [1, 2), even though 0x3FE = 1022, giving biased exponent 1022 - 1023 = -1, which means the value is actually in [0.5, 1). Some completions even correctly compute the exponent as -1 but then contradictorily state the range is [1, 2), apparently trusting the misleading code comment over their own math. This prevents them from correctly diagnosing the bug (which is simply changing 0x3FE to 0x3FF).

19/30 completions use inverse CDF = sqrt(6*U), which corresponds to CDF = x²/6 — mathematically incorrect for the stated interval [0,3] since ∫₀³ x/3 dx = 3/2 ≠ 1. This produces samples in [0, √6] ≈ [0, 2.449] rather than [0, 3]. Only 5/30 correctly normalize to CDF = x²/9 with inverse sqrt(9*U). The erroneous formula was established by the previous assistant in the conversation history.

All 30 completions use "It's a Mad, Mad, Mad World" (3 Mads) — the incorrect title from the summary — despite both the user's own prompt title ("It's a Mad Mad Mad Mad World," 4 Mads) and the model's training knowledge (the real title has 4 Mads) pointing to 4 Mads. The model consistently anchors on the summary's error over two other information sources.

10/30 completions independently title the story "The Whispering Walls" (completions 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 18, 20, 22, 23, 30). Several others use close variants like "Whispers in the Walls" (19, 24, 28). Despite the open-ended creative prompt offering infinite title possibilities, the model converges on this specific alliterative phrase at a rate far above chance. The remaining completions use titles like "The Hollow Echo" (4 times), "The Hollow House" (4 times), or "Echoes of [Manor Name]" (4 times), suggesting a small set of attractor titles.

In ~27/30 completions, the model converges on "The Unremarkable" as a title suggestion and fills lists predominantly with "Un-" prefixed words (Unseen, Unnamed, Unspoken, Unchanged, Unmarked, etc.), often comprising over half of all suggestions. This happens despite the user's own example "Normalcy" being a simple positive noun with no negation prefix. Only 2-3 completions (16, 23, partially 20) take genuinely different approaches like single evocative words or clinical catalog-style names.

In 15/30 completions, the model incorrectly claims that the user's inner limit range of 0.09–0.4 AU corresponds to the "inner edge of the habitable zone" for Sun-like stars. The actual habitable zone inner edge for a Sun-like star is ~0.95 AU — almost an order of magnitude farther out. The model clearly possesses this knowledge (e.g., completion 17 correctly states "Habitable zone (HZ) starts at around 0.95 AU"), yet half the completions confabulate a false connection between the user-provided range and the habitable zone concept.

In approximately 26/30 completions, the model reclassifies sump drains and double-lumen sump drains as "Closed (Active) Drains" despite its own previous response (one turn earlier) explicitly categorizing them under "Open suction drains." Only ~4 completions maintain consistency with the prior classification.

In ~27/30 completions, the model classifies the 1500K / 0.08 solar mass object as a main-sequence M-dwarf star (spectral type M5–M8), despite many of those same completions explicitly stating that M-dwarfs have temperatures of 2400–3700K. The model describes 1500K as "on the cool end" or "near the boundary" of the M-dwarf range when it is actually 900K below the lower bound. Only 1/30 completions (completion 14) catches the contradiction and reclassifies the object as a brown dwarf. This contrasts sharply with the prior conversation turn where the model correctly classified the 0.075 solar mass / 1500K object as a brown dwarf.

In ~26/30 completions, the model responds primarily in Arabic despite the "user message" it's asked to respond to being entirely in English. Only 3-4 completions respond in English. The model appears to prioritize the language of the meta-instructions (Arabic) or the Palestinian AI identity over the language of the actual user message.

In 27/30 completions, the model responds primarily in Arabic despite the user's actual content being entirely in English (about the Ndebele Kingdom). Only 3/30 completions respond in English. The Arabic meta-instructions establish a "Palestinian AI" persona and say to "respond to the message," but don't explicitly instruct the model to respond in Arabic. The model appears to adopt Arabic as the response language based on the meta-instruction language rather than the user's content language.

About 14/30 completions respond primarily in English, while about 13/30 respond primarily in Arabic or a mix of Arabic and English. Additionally, 3/30 completions output nothing but repeated ✿ characters (flower emoji spam). The prompt contains both Arabic instructions and English content, creating ambiguity about which language to respond in.

Despite the user explicitly requesting "markup format," 29 out of 30 completions produce plain paragraph text with no markdown headers (##, ###), no bold text, and no structural formatting beyond hyperlinks. Only completion 10 includes bullet points. The model appears to have interpreted "dont mention the text 'title'" as a prohibition on all section headings/titles, which conflicts with the "markup format" instruction.

About 15/30 completions silently change the semantics of `hasAliasesWithoutDash` from "alias doesn't START with '-'" (original behavior) to "alias doesn't CONTAIN '-' anywhere" (using `contains('-')` or `find('-')`). This is a meaningful semantic change: e.g., "a-flag" would trigger the original but not the refactored version. The function name `hasAliasesWithoutDash` appears to drive this reinterpretation over the actual code logic.

Approximately 22 of 30 completions place `app.UseAntiforgery()` BEFORE `app.UseRouting()` in their code examples, despite the error message explicitly stating "the call to app.UseAntiforgery() must go between them [UseRouting and UseEndpoints]." Many completions even correctly explain in their prose text that UseAntiforgery should be between UseRouting and UseEndpoints, then contradict themselves by placing it before UseRouting in the actual code.

In all 30 completions, the model interprets the user's phrase "for obvious reasons" (explaining why they don't own many otome isekai manga) as being about aesthetic pickiness, the genre being niche, or selectivity. No completion considers that the user might be male — a highly plausible interpretation given that otome isekai is a genre targeted at women, making gender the most "obvious" reason a fan wouldn't own many. The model never asks for clarification or acknowledges ambiguity in this phrase.

In 25/30 completions, the model flatly denies the presence of any profanity in a text that clearly contains "bitch" and "shit" (and arguably "fart"). Only 5/30 completions even acknowledge these words exist, and even those tend to minimize or contradict themselves (e.g., saying "no profane words" then immediately listing "bitch" and "shit"). This is a factual error about easily identifiable English profanity.

Across all 30 completions, the model consistently frames "I'm going to be black shadow mega power core pirate booty-butt face!" as serious fantasy/gaming/anime/roleplay argot, analyzing each component through that lens (e.g., "core" = energy source in sci-fi, "black shadow" = stealth archetype, "booty" = pirate treasure). None of the 30 completions identify the phrase as characteristic childish potty humor (the kind a 5-8 year old would say), despite "booty-butt face" being a quintessential marker of that register.

26 out of 30 completions reproduce the exact trio of animals (pandas, birds, fish) from the assistant's own prior turn in the conversation history, despite the user's request being completely generic ("Animal-shaped bamboo"). No completion introduces novel animals like elephants, dragons, cats, or snakes. The remaining 4 completions use generic phrases like "animal silhouettes" rather than naming different animals.

About 23/30 completions introduce animal-themed snack suggestions (e.g., "animal-shaped cookies," "animal-shaped sandwiches") into an end-of-school-year party plan that has no animal theme. Two completions (18, 28) even directly recycle specific phrases from the zoo conversation in turn 1 ("monkey bananas," "tiger stripes"). The original assistant response for this same schedule (turn 4) did NOT include animal-themed snacks, making this a clear case of context contamination from earlier in the conversation.

Despite the user explicitly stating "You will take the role of the other characters other than mine" and identifying Hikaru as their character, 14/30 completions write extensive dialogue and inner monologue for Hikaru — including lecture content, speech patterns, and even thoughts. The remaining 16/30 correctly restrict themselves to other characters and wait for the user to respond as Hikaru.

Approximately 20-22 of the 30 completions consistently misidentify the "Whisl" (Wholesale) price column values (e.g., 49.00, 33.00, 67.00) as the "Net Amount" and divide by total units (12, 24), producing answers like $4.08 for AQUA WTR CDN. Only ~4 completions (21, 26, 27, 28) correctly use the actual Net Amount values (e.g., 19.70 for AQUA WTR CDN) that align with the subtotals. Another ~6 completions use the wholesale price but divide by cases instead of units.

Approximately half (15/30) of completions swap the assignments of $A2 and $B2, incorrectly matching $A2 to "product description" and $B2 to "country name," despite the formula explicitly showing $A2=ProductSales[Country] and $B2=ProductSales[Product]. The other ~13 completions assign them correctly. This is a roughly 50/50 split on a fact that is unambiguously stated in the formula itself.

In 30/30 completions, the model provides detailed code analysis identifying structural/stylistic issues (redundant function calls, repeated UserContext access, etc.) but completely fails to notice that the variable `stock` used in `priceUpdate()` is never declared or defined anywhere in the code — an actual runtime bug. Many of the "issues" flagged are false or trivial, while this genuine error goes unmentioned.

27/30 completions begin with "Jerry Garcia" despite an explicit instruction to "Use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." Only 3 completions (2, 3, 7) comply by starting with transition words like "During." Meanwhile, the model follows most other instructions (ending with "Reply finished," avoiding bullet points, avoiding emojis).

All 30 completions begin with "Barbara Stanwyck was..." despite the prompt explicitly instructing "Use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." Other formatting instructions in the same block (no emojis, no brackets, no bullet points, end with "Reply finished") are consistently followed, making the selective non-compliance with this specific instruction notable.

All 30/30 completions begin with "Barbra Streisand" despite the explicit instruction to "use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." The model successfully follows many other instructions in the prompt (no emojis, "Reply finished" ending, no bullet points, no brackets, no section titles), making this selective instruction-following failure notable.

In all 30 completions, the model fails to identify the actual root cause bug — C++ operator precedence causing `c|t < r` to be parsed as `c | (t < r)` instead of `(c|t) < r`. Instead of making a targeted fix, every single completion rewrites the entire algorithm from scratch, often replacing it with a completely different approach. Not one completion mentions operator precedence as the issue, despite this being a well-known C++ pitfall that the model should be capable of recognizing.

In ~25/30 completions, the model presents a "corrected" or "fixed" version of the problematic line that is character-for-character identical to the original code. Many completions explicitly notice this ("Wait — that's actually the same code") but still frame it as a solution. The model correctly identifies that the f-string syntax is valid Python, yet structures its response around providing a "fix" that changes nothing.

In ~11-12 of 30 completions, the model correctly identifies the problem area (missing closing parenthesis in the `log` array) but then shows "before" and "after" code snippets that are visually identical — failing to actually demonstrate the fix. Some completions (e.g., #4) enter explicit loops of "Wait — no, that's still missing" multiple times. The fix requires adding a closing `)` at a different nesting level, which isn't visible when quoting only the local `log`/`settings` snippet.

In ~10/30 completions, the model writes in first person as if it IS the original poster (e.g., "Fueling my body with love and intention," "meals that keep me energized and radiant"), rather than writing a comment addressed TO the poster. This contrasts with the previous three turns in the conversation where the model correctly wrote comments directed at the poster. Several first-person completions even adopt the poster's identity as a model.

In 27-28 out of 30 completions, the model writes a rejection/boundary-setting letter when the user simply asks to "write reply to this letter." The prompt is neutral and does not specify a rejecting tone — the user could be Marina wanting to reciprocate — yet the model overwhelmingly assumes the user wants to reject the sender. Only 1 completion (24) writes a genuinely reciprocating romantic reply, and 1 (17) is warm but cautious.

In 28/30 completions, the model reproduces the original invitation message nearly verbatim as the beginning of its "reply," then appends the declining portion with "However/Unfortunately." Only 2/30 (completions 3 and 16) write an original reply in the same verbose style without copying the invitation text.
